title: The Three Dharma Seals
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: The talk explores the concept of the Two Truths in Buddhism, which reveals that our everyday reality is interconnected with a deeper, unconditioned reality. Understanding this interrelation can help us uncover the truth about ourselves and the world around us. By recognizing the impermanence of all things, including our own sense of self, we can begin to let go of attachments and perceptions that cause suffering, ultimately leading to freedom and peace.

sentences.text: Good evening, everybody.
Thank you for being here.
This evening I'm doing part one of a two-part little seminar, so next week we'll hear what I think is a continuation of this topic.
To me these are sets of foundational teachings of the Buddha.
The first one we're going to talk about tonight is called the Three Dharma Seals.
In some lineages it's referred to as the Three Marks of Existence.
Next week I'll continue with what I think is part of this set, known as the Three Doors of Liberation.
I want to say first of all that I hope these fundamental teachings are an invitation for exploration rather than something to believe in.
The teachings, the sutras, the words, they're all tools for each of us to study the Self.
Each of us has to discover those truths within our own set of conditions, so these are just offerings to ponder and try out and see what you think of them.
I may stop for comments as we go along with some of the things I'm going to talk about.
Before we delve into the main topic, oh, I should say that I called this talk Uncovering the Three Dharma Seals.
I forgot.
Before we delve into the main topic for this evening, though, I want to mention something called the Two Truths in Buddhism.
As we discuss the other topics, maybe this notion of the Two Truths will help inform the rest of what I'm talking about.
In Buddhist understanding, we live in two realms really simultaneously.
They're not exactly two, but we're going to say they're two realms.
The first is the realm of the conditioned, our historic realm that we're used to living in.
We go to the grocery store, we drive the car.
All those things are part of our conditioned historic realm, where we have a distinct boundary of a body and a life that we are carrying out.

I remember some old Zen story about somebody who was stating to the teacher that, no, no, I have no self or something, and the teacher grabbed his nose and said, well, who's pinching your nose then, or something.
Anyway, we can't discount that we have boundaries on a body and all those things.
But there is another realm, and it's called the realm of the unconditioned.
Some people call it the ultimate realm, the ultimate dimension.
Thich Nhat Hanh, who is my root teacher, called it that.
They're interrelated, two sides of the same coin, and they're really never apart.
There isn't a possible way that you can have one without the other.
In the Heart Sutra, we hear, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form.
In the conditioned realm, there are many concepts and many constructs, and these are integrated into our sense of separateness and our self-identity.
These may be coming from our thoughts, our perceptions, our constructs, and we use those: things like traffic laws and rules at the library or whatever.
In the teachings of the Buddha, however, all of these perceptions, all of these constructs, also live in the realm of the unconditioned, the ultimate realm.
A common analogy that Thich Nhat Hanh always liked to use to illustrate this was waves and the ocean.
We are waves.
We have an individual form, if you will, part of the time, and it's always changing, but we're never not the ocean.
It's just a way to think about things.

It's this understanding that allows us to consider how, for a time, we do have our own life span, but truly, we're also always part of the ocean, ultimately free from coming and going, and from birth and death, which we'll talk about a little more.

As I move into our discussion, I want to give some examples from my own life and perspective about living in both of these realms, and how sometimes we can be offered a glimpse that somehow may jolt us into seeing that we're really in both of these at the same time.
These examples that I'm going to offer help me open the hand of thought, as a famous teacher, Uchiyama Roshi, said.
For those who don't know him, he was the teacher of another really famous living teacher, Shohaku Okumura, who is a really well-known Dogen scholar.
Anyway, these examples are not earth-shattering at all.
They're just things that come to mind.
They're just things that somehow caught me, revealing this pattern of thought that perpetuates my mind and influences who I am.
I want to emphasize that I'm not trying so hard anymore to get rid of unwanted qualities.
I'm just allowing myself to see more and more in an objective way: aha, there I go again.
I think the more we can objectively notice these characteristics, the more we are able to uncover them.
Uchiyama Roshi loves to remind us that there are often these constant thoughts he calls brain secretions.
When we think of them in that way, it's helpful, because we realize that they're human things, but they're not the ultimate truth.
They're just stuff that we're thinking.
I remember one time, some of you may know our teacher that founded Red Cedar, Norman Fischer, his wife is also a teacher.
She was talking about how one time she just decided to scribble down her thoughts just for a little bit, just to see how wise they were.
She said they were just this mumbo jumbo of things, one subject after another.
It's really good to be aware of that stuff that's going on all the time that's not necessarily the most wise and the most permanent.
Anyway, it's like this poem that I found the other day.
I think I read it in our seven o'clock thing, but it was by an old Zen teacher, [unclear: "sure do"].
It's just this little short thing that says:
*Cloud of distress is just cloud of distress.
Rain of sadness is just rain of sadness.
Storm of anger is just storm of anger.
Without being cleaned up, opening the hand of thought, just sit as the boundless sky is the boundless sky, including the clouds.*
So we can watch things coming and going and not try to make them go away, but also just realize that they're constant.
When we examine Buddhist teachings, there are two realms, as always.
Both of those are always interrelated, and they illustrate understanding from one perspective or another.
If you are interested in reading sutras, you've maybe read different sutras that go back and forth with the explanations.

Something really helpful to keep in mind: I know Thich Nhat Hanh was doing a commentary on the Lotus Sutra, and he illustrated how it's really good to see what perspective the narrator is coming from, because sometimes they're in the historical realm and other times they're in the ultimate realm.
They go back and forth, and sometimes it's really confusing.
So it's just something to keep in mind as you're reading through these sutras: where are they coming from?
Are they talking about the historic realm or the ultimate realm?
I'll talk about that more a little bit later.
The reason that we want to uncover this ultimate realm, little by little, is because that's the place of freedom.
That's the place that is unhindered by the thoughts and going to the grocery store and figuring out what to buy and that kind of stuff.
So we'll just hold that.
But they give us a chance to see beyond our identity that we've created, which is often very narrow and confining.
And it also gives us a chance to transform the historical realm that often leads us to suffering.
So tonight, when I look at these three dharma seals, they really are seals.
They're called seals because they're really seals of authentication.
It's said that if a teaching doesn't bear these three signs, these three, I shouldn't say signs, these three seals, then it's not a teaching of the Buddha.
So they're things we can think about and use to gauge, when we read something: does that contain these three seals that we're going to talk about?
The first seal is impermanence.
The second seal is no self, which we'll talk about.
And the third seal is nirvana.
But in some schools of Buddhism, they say the third seal is suffering.
Some schools use one and some use another, so we'll talk about that a little bit more: why, and how you can hold both of those.
Impermanence is the first Dharma seal.
If we look at this on a day-to-day, even moment-by-moment basis, we intellectually understand that that's true.
And yet I'm not sure if we're really getting this fully, or at least me.
Sometimes we can catch ourselves betraying our understanding of this.
One of the fundamental verses from the Buddha, people are very encouraged to repeat and think about, recollect every day.
It's called the Five Remembrances.
Does anybody know those?
Ariel knows, Ken knows, yeah, Echo.
A lot of people I know practice with this every day.
These five remembrances are talking about our conditioned world.
And they say:
*I am of a nature to grow old.
There is no way to escape growing old.
I am of a nature to have ill health.
There is no way to escape having ill health.
I am of a nature to die.
There is no way to escape death.
All that is dear to me and everyone I love are of a nature to change.
There is no way to escape being separated from them.
My actions are my only true belongings.
I cannot escape the consequences of my actions.
My actions are the ground on which I stand.*
When we first encounter this verse, we may feel kind of repelled by it.
It sounds so glum and pessimistic.
So we think, why is this helpful to hear?
I just wondered if you have any comment about that as we go along, what your first impression was or why you think maybe they're helpful.
Yeah, yeah.
Exactly.
Yeah.
John?
Yeah, right.
Right.
Thanks.
Yeah, so when we encounter this,

Thich Nhat Hanh says the five remembrances help us make friends with our fears about growing old, about getting sick, about being abandoned and dying, and maybe about our craving and attachment to things, as you were talking about.
They really can be a mindfulness bell to help us appreciate the wonders of life right now available.
But then Thich Nhat Hanh says, well, then why would Avalokiteshvara in the Heart Sutra say there is no birth and death?
Why would the Buddha say that we are of a nature to die if there is no birth and death?
Because in the five remembrances, the Buddha is using the tool of the relative truth, the conditioned world.
It's reality.
It is the truth in this world that we're living in.
But he's also aware of this deeper truth, this absolute truth, the ultimate reality where there is no birth and death, which we'll talk about as we go along.
So I think the more I recite this, the more it helps me also touch that ultimate reality, the reality that is deeper than birth and death, coming and going, you and me.
But first, I think we have to recognize and accept the reality of the conditioned world.
It's like, I don't know, thinking about suffering.
We can't really go around it.
This is like that.
We need to be able to see how things are right now.
We need to see that this body is not going to go on living forever.
As humans we habitually deepen and deepen our brain's neural pathways, creating what we like to think of as our identity, continuing forever.
And Uchiyama Roshi says these tools to practice with give us different pathways.

I was listening to another Dharma talk too, where he was talking about all these ways we have such deep neural pathways, again and again and again, that when we have those so established, that's when we have no beginner's mind with that anymore.
We skip over it and just think, oh, yeah, I know that.
If it's an apple, if it's whatever it is, we don't even really see it.
So some of these tools that the Buddha offered are really tools to help develop different pathways, as we practice again and again.
So here's a couple of silly examples of me really believing in permanence and liking to live there, and being a little shocked when I found out that I really was doing that.
The first one I remember: we've moved several times.
And this time, where we are now, when we moved in, there was this great big huge hedge of blackberries.
And the neighbors offered, oh, I've got some poison if you want to get rid of those, or they wanted us to cut them out.
And, uh-oh, am I still standing okay?
So anyway, I felt very protective of the blackberries as soon as we moved in because the birds especially love them.
They love that hedge and it's their refuge.
It made me want to really protect them.
So we're really good at keeping them cut down, so the neighbors aren't too mad.
But anyway, we started thinking about moving at one time.
And I thought, oh, I can't move.
I have to protect these.
I have to protect the hedge and the birds.
And no, I don't want to have that go away.
And then all of a sudden I realized that I was not going to be around forever.
I couldn't, no matter how long I stayed in the house, it would come to an end.
I couldn't be there to protect them all the time.
And the hedges aren't going to be there forever either.
So it was just: wait a minute, how long did I think I was going to be able to protect them all?
Another thing that was really, well, I'll just tell you the story.
My dad, a couple of years before he died, we went to the store.
He wanted to get some clothes, including underwear.
He finally figured out, okay, he wanted this kind of underwear.
He grabbed it and put it in the cart, and right away I grabbed a second package.
I said, "Oh, here, Dad, just throw these in.
You might as well get those while we're here."
And he turned around and he said, "Honey, how long do you think I'm going to be around?"
It made me realize that I hadn't even thought of that.
And he was really practical.
He knew that I hadn't.
So anyway, it's things like that.
I think sometimes we have a little realization, but my thoughts just want me to continue forever, or whatever.
But anyway, I think our minds betray us.
We can intellectually tell ourselves, "Yes, yes, I know things are impermanent."
But when it comes right down to it, our misperceptions come to the surface.
So what can we do about this?
Just have awareness, just have a recollection.
I think it's both awareness in the moment and also a recollection of some of these stories that happened to us, when we think, "Oh, yeah."
The next Dharma seal is called No Self.
So what does this mean?
Does it mean that I am nothing, ultimately?
Does it mean that I'm not a person living in this world?
As we talk about emptiness next week, we'll also talk a little further about what we are made of, and how this is in addition to or beyond who we think we are.
Think is a big clue.
Our identity has been carved out again and again, mostly by our mind.
Thay, Thich Nhat Hanh, often says that we are made of non-self elements.
When we talk about emptiness, we'll talk about that a little bit more.
But in fact, there is no identity that we can find that is who we think we are.
So myself, Desiree, is made of all non-self elements and bits and pieces of really all of existence.
We know scientifically that we're calcium and iron and we came from the stars, and all of these things are actually pretty wonderful.
So it's not a question of whether I exist or not.
It's a recognition of all these things that came together for me to appear, for my manifestation to appear.
It doesn't take long to see how my mother and father are in me, and how their karma and their actions are also in me.
Sometimes it's very clear: "Oh, okay, that was from my dad."
But I want to talk about it a little more.
This subject is really the same to me as emptiness, which we're going to talk about next week, so we'll investigate this a little bit more.
Sometimes I'm shocked again by things that don't fit who I think I am, just some fleeting things.
For instance, have you ever been to the dentist and had your x-rays taken, and then they show you the skull with these teeth and you think, "Oh, my gosh, is that me?"
It just doesn't fit with our perception of me.
I think all of those things are really good for us, actually.
Anyway, that's a little one.
But I had a jolt like that one time that really pulled me out of my me identity and shocked me in different ways, in terms of who I thought me was.
It happened quite a few years ago now.
We got a microscope from my son, and he was probably eight or nine or something.
I wanted to show him these discoveries on the slide.
So first I went out to the planter outside and I got this little vial of stagnant water.
I put it on the slide and we looked in there, and there were all these little creatures, all these little bacteria and whatever living creatures in there.
The first thing I felt was compassion for all of these little living things.
I realized that I don't usually think of them.
I don't usually acknowledge them because I'm not usually looking at them.
But I saw them, and as soon as I saw them, my thought was, "Oh, I want to take care of them and be careful not to harm them and put them back into the planter when we're done."
Then I decided to show my son some red blood cells from my body living there.
I felt like they were renting space from me.
So I pricked my finger and I put a drop of blood on the slide.
We saw these little organisms, these little red blood cells.
It was really astonishing.
We looked at the slide and they were vibrating.
They were alive, just for a few seconds.
And then they slowly stopped moving.
It was such a weird thing, because then I realized that the red blood cells were me.
And just for a few seconds they were alive.
No border, at least on the inside, separated them from me.
But secondly, I saw that I had a strange notion about [unclear: "gathering them"].
I felt like I had more compassion for the creatures on the slide from the planter than I did for me.
I just had this thing like, "Oh, that was just me."
That was also a strange juxtaposition, I thought.
It was like seeing them as separate at first, but then understanding that they were me.
Some kind of judgment, about "oh, that's just my blood."
And it reminds me of Dogen's Genjokoan, where he was talking about all the things that live in their own environment: the birds flying in the sky, in the air, the fish in the water.
If the bird leaves that environment, it dies at once.
And if the fish leaves the water, did I say that right, then they die at once.
And I thought, oh, my red blood cells, if we take them out of their environment, they die too.
But I saw that everything is really living and dying at the same time, each in its own element.
And all of these pieces are me.
I truly have no separate identity.
And neither do the red blood cells or the vast network of sentient and non-sentient beings that make up me.
Somehow I had a deeper appreciation for these cells that were living as individual cells and at the same time also interconnected within this larger structure that was me.
So I think it's like that with everything.
We have a separate cell that gets up and makes breakfast and goes about the day.
And yet we really have no true boundaries if we're looking deeply at everything that made us up.
It's true that the elements are living and dying continuously, every moment, impermanent, making room for new manifestations both within this body and without.
Being alive and then not alive is happening all the time to all sentient beings, from single cells to human beings, ever arising, ever passing away.
But if we touch the ground of being, our ultimate nature, still right here, nothing is really lost.
And I think I'll talk about that more next week.
So before I continue to the next topic, does anybody want to share an experience, a similar thing that jolted them out of their identity?
Ariel?
Yeah.
Right.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And way less permanent, I mean, everything.
I really like that idea that everything in me, outside of me, everything is living and dying.
All these things are living and dying all the time.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Kind of time and space.
So, yeah.
Finally, this evening, I want to talk about the third Dharma seal, sometimes the third and fourth, depending on where you are practicing.
This Dharma seal is either called Nirvana, or in some schools, it is suffering.
As we talk a little bit more, we'll see that really they're two sides of the same coin.
But well, I won't go on, so I'll just continue.
The first Dharma seals that we talked about, impermanence and no self, are universal.
They're marks of things in the conditioned world, and they are on the same level as each other.
But Thich Nhat Hanh explains that to put suffering on that same level is an error.
Because in this conditioned world, it's not difficult to see, for instance, the table or the tree in the forest, all of those things.
It doesn't have a separate self.
In fact, it is constantly changing and all these new forms are growing out of it.
You can look at the tree or the table and see the tree and see the woodcutter that was in there and see the rain and see the sun.
So it's easy to see that it has no self in that way, no separate self.
But is it suffering?
He asks.
It's part of this world, but it's not necessarily suffering.
So suffering, Thich explains, is not a given.
It's not necessarily constant.
Nirvana is its companion, the other side of the coin.
Thich explains Nirvana to mean, he says, an extinction.
And you ask, extinction of what?
It's extinction of notions and ideas.
So when we talk about Nirvana, that doesn't mean some faraway place in heaven or something that's perfect.
It means that there aren't ideas, notions and ideas, in Nirvana, in that freedom, that place.
So most all the time we cause our own suffering.

When we place a permanent attribute onto something and are then attached to it, the Buddha taught impermanence and no self so that we wouldn't get caught up in those kinds of signs, which we'll talk about more next week.
But from a worldly point of view, there is the suffering of impermanence and no self.
But from the point of view of the true nature, the ultimate dimension, concepts are silenced and at peace.
So Nirvana is an underlying reality that's often obscured by suffering.
And there's a note there that in the Southern transmission, the three Dharma Seals are often said to be impermanent, suffering and no self.
But in the Samyukta Agama, the Buddha taught impermanence, no self and Nirvana as the three Dharma Seals.

And in the introduction commentary by Shohaku Okumura about a book by Dogen called [unclear: "Zui Monkey"], he discusses four Dharma Seals and says that it includes suffering and Nirvana, each in their own category.
But these, he says, are not really four separate items, but rather one unified message from the Buddha.
He says impermanence and no self are the true reality of all things.
When we're blind to these truths and live based on the ideas of permanence and a fixed independent self, everything in our lives becomes suffering.
However, when we awaken to the true reality instead, our life becomes Nirvana.
I liked that statement.
They're just two sides of the same coin.
So whichever version you like, whichever version you resonate with, that's great.
And the exploration comes back really to the four noble truths: suffering, the causes of suffering, the cessation of suffering and the path.
It's all really connected.
The more I practice, the more I see that my mind, my thoughts are truly the cause of much of my suffering, probably all of my suffering.
Suffering is not the same as having pain or having physical discomfort.
I can have pain in my leg, for instance, which I had a lot of, especially when I was younger.
Yeah, OK, that was pain.
But then I start ruminating about things with my mind, such as, oh, no, why today?
Why today of all days, I really wanted to go out with my friends on the outing.
Why does this always happen to me?
I couldn't, it goes on and on and on.
Yeah, so that becomes the suffering.
Emotional suffering makes up a huge amount of our suffering.
I think I can add on a huge amount of fretting over something that is so often not even the truth.
Here's another silly example.
Parents can relate to this.
A few years ago, when my son was still at home, he was out late and I started worrying, once you start.
I woke up and he wasn't home and it was getting later and later.
Then I started worrying more and my mind was going round and round.
I think I texted him once or twice, no reply.
So I was getting more and more frantic.
I texted him again.
This time I got a reply, and he said, "Mom, I'm home.
I was asleep in bed.
I was being so quiet so I wouldn't disturb you."
Anyway, he never lets me forget that.
I'm not saying that something couldn't have happened.
Things happen, but it doesn't help to fret and worry about stuff.
And I'm telling all of you as if I don't do that, but of course I do.
But yes, your mind can just take off.
That kind of energy, not just fretting but ruminating, where you're not with what is, not with the way things are, uses a lot of energy.
I've really noticed that.
Sometimes I can think about something and start clinging to it or being attached to it, and it's a lot of energy.
If I can tell myself even just to let it go for one second, I really can physically feel free.
Just for that little bit, anyway.
We spend a lot of time in emotional responses to these thoughts, which are often not based on what's happening.
We make decisions about other people based on our assumptions, and our misperceptions lead us to fear, to insecurity, to anger.
I think you've probably all heard the Zen story about the fisherman who was out on the water in the fog.
He saw another fishing boat, and at first he couldn't see it too well, but it was coming closer and closer and closer.
He was thinking, surely this person is going to see me at some point and stop.
But no, the boat just kept coming and coming.
So then he started getting more and more angry.
What is he doing?
Why is he not seeing me?
Finally the boat slammed into him.
He was so angry, and he looked in the boat and no one was there.
I think that happens so often, though maybe not exactly like that.
We can rile ourselves up so much with a perception that we think is true and correct, and it's not at all.
We find so often that things are not the way they seem.
So the Buddha taught us not to be fooled by what we perceive.
He told [unclear: "Sabuddhi"], where there is perception, there is deception.
A useful phrase for me from Thich Nhat Hanh is, "Are you sure?"
I didn't like that phrase at first.
I didn't like all the things that hit home.
I noticed one time, with a book that he wrote called *Anger*, my first thought was, oh, no, that's not for me.
And all those things, even words, I think I talked about before, certain words that I didn't like, because I didn't really want to look at them.
But this was one of the phrases: "Are you sure?"
Lately I'm using it a lot, because so often, when I honestly think I'm right, I think, oh, maybe not.
So often it happens that I see I wasn't right or sure.
Sometimes people think of being in the world of suffering or being in the world of nirvana for a lifetime.

But whether you question or wonder about reincarnation from lifetime to lifetime, as we've talked about a little bit, even in our own bodies, we mentioned living and dying are happening all the time, and suffering and nirvana are present.
Also, when I think about being in the realm of suffering, I see that this can be transformed in a moment, and vice versa.
I've found myself in a realm of suffering, or what I would call a realm of hell, in an instant, by my own actions.
So I think heaven and hell are not reserved for the end of a lifetime or the beginning of another one.
They are in the present moment.
It's possible to be in a realm of hell right now, and it's also possible to be in a realm of nirvana right now.
So our thoughts and actions really determine where we're at.
By letting go of my ideas and notions and my incorrect perceptions, I can step into a realm of freedom.
Of course, for me it's just a constant back and forth.
But by watching how my mind works, I can have a little bit more choice on where I want to go, or where I want to be.
I think Chris the other day had a question: where do you abide right now?
Where are you abiding?
I think that's a great question to really think about as we're going through the day.
Next week we'll talk a little bit more about our mind and perceptions and labels and signs and all of these things that can trap us a little bit more or let us be free.
So I want to bring up one last quote by Thich Nhat Hanh.
He says:
*Suffering is not a basic element of existence.
It's a feeling.
When we insist on something that is impermanent and without a self being permanent and having a self, we suffer.*
We talked about that.
We can really pay attention to this phrase in our life and, from a deep standpoint, perhaps see more and more into this truth.
We're often resisting something that is, or wanting it to be different.
The Buddha taught that when suffering is present, we have to identify it, and then we can take steps to transform it.
He did not teach us that suffering is a given always.
Thich Nhat Hanh continues:
*We practice the three Dharma Seals to realize liberation.
If you memorize a five thousand page book on the three Dharma Seals, but do not apply it to the teachings, do not apply those teachings during your daily life, the book will be of no use.
Only by using intelligence and putting the teachings into practice can they bring you happiness.*
So please bring your practice into your own life and into your own experiences.
The Buddhist teachings are jewels, but we have to dig deeper in order to touch them fully.
So thank you for listening to the talk.
And this evening, I think, oh my gosh, it's time.
That's the first time I've ever gotten over.
Okay, so anyway, they are in.

verbatim.text: So good evening everybody, thank you for being here. So this evening I'm going to be doing part one of a two-part little seminar, so next week we'll hear what I think is kind of a continuation of this topic, so we'll continue with that next week. So to me these are sets of foundational teachings of the Buddha, and the first one that we're going to talk about tonight is called the Three Dharma Seals. In some lineages it's referred to as the Three Marks of Existence, and next week I'll continue with what I think is part of this set known as the Three Doors of Liberation. So I want to say first of all that I hope that these fundamental teachings are an invitation for exploration rather than something to believe in. They're really there, you know, the teachings, the sutras, the words, they're all tools for each of us to be able to study the Self. Each of us has to discover that those truths within our own set of conditions, and so these are, you know, they're just offerings to kind of ponder and try out and see what you think of them. So I may stop for comments as we go along with some of the things I'm going to talk about. So before we delve into the main topic, oh I should say that I called this talk Uncovering the Three Dharma Seals, I forgot.

And so before we delve into the main topic for this evening though, I want to mention something called the Two Truths in Buddhism.
